context: Wilde to George Ives, postmarked 22 February 1900, Paris. Nine months before his death, reviewing Ives's book to his face and then telling him off twice over — for the secretiveness that made him omit his address, and for the cab-drivers' eating house. Wilde wants somewhere they can talk.
quote:
Hotel d’Alsace, Rue des Beaux Arts

My dear George — Thank you very much for the book — it is powerfully written — Of course it lacks Style — but between Truth and Style there is always a désaccord — unless one is a poet. The ideas in the book are excellent — but the mode of presentation lacks charm — The book stimulates but does not win one — But I am glad to have it.

I know you __intended__ to put your address in your telegram — but the habit — the bad habit — of secretiveness made you omit it — What a warning!

I have no doubt your little eating house, where the cochers de fiacre go, is delightful to you — but, really George, it is hardly the place to invite others to — You should keep it as a private luxury — a cheap haven of unrest —

When you come again to Paris I hope you will breakfast with _me_ — I know lots of nice, quiet, seemly places — where we can talk — Rien n’est sacré à un cocher de fiacre — Besides, they are revolting personally.

Bosie is over here — with his brother — they are in deep mourning and the highest spirits. The English are like that. —

I am delighted you are interested in the cover of your book — I always _began_ with the cover — Ever yours Oscar
original_provenance: Read at HRC 2700, images 5-8. Two bifolia, eight sides: image 5 gives sides 1 (right) and 4 (left), image 6 the inner opening 2-3, image 7 sides 5 (right) and 8 (left), image 8 the inner opening 6-7. Images 9-10 are the envelope. Written on Grand Cafe, 4 Boulevard des Capucines paper with the printed letterhead struck through by a long diagonal stroke and 'Hotel d'Alsace' written over it, on both bifolia. Emphasis: '_began_' on the last side, in the same ink and the width of the word. The volume sets it in italic and keeps it. A third mark, missed then confirmed: '_me_' in 'breakfast with _me_' on side 6. The volume italicises it; I did not check the sheet there, because the OCR mirror gave no reason to look. Confirmed by Lovelle 2026-08-10, who also confirms it is the only underline on that opening. 'me' is a word he underlines elsewhere - doubly, in the Harris letter of 13 June 1897. Emphasis, Null: nothing else is underlined. Not 'Style' (twice), not 'Truth', not 'désaccord', not 'Talk', and not 'Rien n'est sacré à un cocher de fiacre'. The volume italicises the French and the désaccord; that is its convention for foreign matter, not a mark Wilde made, and this letter is a clean demonstration of the conflation. Emphasis, Double: '__intended__' on side 3 - two parallel strokes in the writing ink at the writing weight, confirmed by Lovelle 2026-08-10 after I flagged them as possibly an emphatic dash. They sit slightly right of the word and run on into blank paper, which is what made them ambiguous at first; they are a double underline. It is the strongest mark in the set - he is pressing on the gap between what Ives meant to do and what he did. The volume sets 'intended' in italic - which corroborates a mark, though it cannot show the doubling, the edition stating in its own preliminaries that it italicises all underlinings without indicating multiple ones. Read with care: at page size the ruled lines of the paper and the show-through from the verso read as underlines under 'Style', 'Truth' and 'talk'; at 3-4x they resolve as ruling, and the stroke over 'talk' resolves as the crossbar of his t, which runs long and is continuous with the letter. 'powerfully' confirmed at 4x. Punctuation: his dashes throughout, restored; the volume replaces most of them with full stops and commas. Envelope (images 9-10): Grand Cafe stationery, 'Angleterre' underlined, to 'George Ives Esq., Royal Societies Club, St James' Street, S.W., London', Paris Nord postmark, London S.W. FE 23 00 on the verso; docketed by Ives 'Feb 23 00' and 'Oscar Wilde' underlined. How the two errors above happened: this entry's statements about what the volume prints were first taken from the OCR text mirror. The mirror is plain text and carries no italics at all, so 'the volume prints it roman' was never a reading - it was an artefact of a format that cannot record the distinction. Corrected 2026-08-10 against a 200dpi render of the printed page. No claim about roman versus italic may rest on the mirror. 1173 - stand, because there the edition read a real difference.
